t19: Everyone gets the same dice in backgammon; what makes the difference is what you do with the roll. The seven principles below are the rules that fastest raise a beginner's win rate.
t21: A single piece on a point can be hit and sent back to the start. Ask yourself one question each turn: "After this move, how many of my pieces are exposed, and what rolls will my opponent need to hit them?"
t22: Leaving blots is not always wrong, but what you gain must be bigger than the risk.
t23: 2. Try to close your home board
t24: Closing points in your home board (last six points) with two pieces makes it hard for captured opponent pieces to re-enter. As you close more points, the time your opponent spends stuck off the board grows.
t25: Especially closing point 5 (the golden point) is considered one of backgammon's most valuable single moves.
t27: If your opponent's home board is well blocked, capturing is more valuable; they'll struggle to re-enter.
t28: If your own home board is open, you're likely to get hit back after capturing.
t29: Hitting when ahead is less risky than when behind.
t31: If you're ahead on the race, reducing contact helps you: move your pieces quickly home and avoid meeting them. This is called a running game.
t32: If you're behind, do the opposite: keep pieces on your opponent's path and wait for hitting chances. For a trailing player, contact is the only realistic way to win; gathering in early locks in defeat.
t34: Stacking six or seven pieces on one point is a wasted resource. Spread pieces give you more opportunities to close points; clumped pieces limit your move options.
t37: The most likely roll to hit a distance is 6 (about 17/36).
t38: The chance of being hit from one space away is 11/36 — that's roughly one in three rolls.
t39: Far distances (greater than 7) are only hit by combinations, probability drops sharply.
t40: 7. In the end game, do the math
t41: When pieces leave contact, the game becomes a pure race. The only question then is: who will take fewer rolls to gather? Roughly counting remaining distance tells you whether you need risky moves or can play safely.
t43: These principles only sink in by playing against real opponents. In SogeGammon you can sit at a table without waiting for a chip, play in short (1 point), classic (5 point), or long (10 point) formats, and measure yourself in ranked ratings.
t45: What's the most important point in backgammon?
t46: Your own home board's point 5. Closing it early directly affects both defense and your opponent's re-entry, making it the single most valuable point.
t47: What should you do when you're behind?
t48: Instead of avoiding contact, seek it out. Keeping pieces on your opponent's path and waiting for hitting chances is the only realistic way to come from behind.
t49: Is leaving a blot always bad?
t50: No. Taking risk to close a point or gain an important position is often the right move; the critical thing is to calculate what the risk is worth.
